title: Blown-In vs Batt Insulation: Which Is Better?
h1: Blown-In vs Batt Insulation: Which Is Better for Your Attic?
description: Blown-in insulation fills gaps and covers irregular attics well, while batts suit open, standard spaces. Compare the two and see which fits your home better.
quick_answer: For most existing attics, blown-in insulation is the better choice because it fills around wiring, ducts and framing without leaving gaps and can be added over clean existing insulation. Batts can be a good fit for open attics with standard joist spacing, new construction or walls. Installation quality matters as much as the type.
body:
Blown-in and batt insulation are the two most common ways to insulate an attic floor. Both can work well. The better choice depends on your attic's layout, what's already up there and how carefully it's installed.

What's the difference between blown-in and batts?

Blown-in insulation (also called loose fill) is fiberglass or cellulose that's blown into the attic through a hose. It settles into an even layer that covers the attic floor, filling around joists, wiring, pipes and other obstacles.

Batt insulation comes in pre-cut blankets, usually fiberglass or mineral wool, sized to fit between standard joist spacing. Batts are laid in by hand and cut to fit around obstacles.

Both blown-in and batt insulation come in fiberglass, and blown-in also comes in cellulose. The format matters most for coverage. The material affects things like moisture handling, settling and fire resistance. A well-installed layer at the right depth will outperform a premium material that's full of gaps, so focus first on coverage and depth, then on material.

Here is how they stack up in a typical attic:

Blown-inBatts
Coverage around obstaclesVery goodDepends on cutting and fit
Adding over old insulationEasyPossible, laid across joists
Installation speed in atticsFast with equipmentSlower in cluttered attics
DIY friendlyNeeds a blowing machineYes, in open spaces
Best forMost existing atticsOpen attics, walls, new framing

Why is blown-in often the better choice for attics?

  • Better coverage. It fills small gaps and irregular spaces that batts can miss.
  • Works around obstacles. Attics with ducts, wiring, a furnace and bracing are easier to cover evenly.
  • Adds easily over existing insulation. If what's there is clean and dry, blown-in can go right on top.
  • Fast installation. A crew can cover a typical attic quickly with a blowing machine.
  • Easy to reach target depth. Depth markers make it simple to confirm coverage.

When do batts make more sense?

  • Open attics with standard joist spacing and few obstacles, where batts fit snugly without much cutting.
  • Walls and floors during new construction or remodels, where cavities are open and uniform.
  • Small areas like knee walls or around an attic hatch.
  • DIY projects in easy-to-reach spaces, since batts don't need a blowing machine.

What are the drawbacks of each?

Blown-in

Loose fill can shift if it's walked on or blown around by strong attic airflow. Cellulose may settle over time and doesn't do well if it gets wet. Blown-in insulation makes it harder to see wiring and joists later, so mark walking paths and important areas.

Batts

Batts only perform as rated when they fill the cavity completely without gaps or compression. Cutting around wiring, pipes and bracing is easy to do poorly. Gaps at the edges, batts squeezed under wires and voids around obstacles all let heat through. Batts also don't fit well in attics with uneven joist spacing.

Which is better for a San Diego home?

Many homes here have low-pitched attics with flex ducts, a furnace and wiring running across the joists. Blown-in insulation handles that kind of space well. Inland homes with hot summer attics benefit from reaching a good, even depth, and blown-in makes that easier.

If your attic has rodent droppings, water damage or matted insulation, don't add anything on top. That material should be removed first, and the space cleaned and sealed.

What else should be done before insulating?

  1. Air seal. Seal gaps around light fixtures, wiring, plumbing and top plates so air doesn't leak through the new insulation.
  2. Protect ventilation. Install baffles so insulation doesn't block soffit vents.
  3. Check recessed lights. Fixtures not rated for insulation contact need clearance or covers.
  4. Insulate the hatch. A bare attic hatch is a common weak spot.
  5. Inspect the ducts. Fix leaks and disconnected runs while the attic is open.

faqs: Is blown-in insulation better than batts?
In most existing attics, yes, because it covers obstacles and gaps more evenly. Batts can perform well in open, standard-spaced attics when installed carefully.
Can I put blown-in insulation over batts?
Yes, if the batts are clean, dry and free of rodent contamination. Blown-in insulation can be added on top to reach the recommended depth.
Some settling is normal, especially with cellulose. Installers account for it by blowing to the proper depth, so the insulation still meets its target after settling.
Is batt insulation easier to install yourself?
In open, easy-to-reach spaces, batts are simpler for DIY because they do not need a blowing machine. Cutting them to fit snugly without gaps or compression is the hard part.
